title: Assessing Pharmacist Awareness of Benzodiazepines’ Long-Term Withdrawal Effects
content: Background: Benzodiazepine withdrawal is well documented, with some patients reporting symptoms that persist long-term. BIND (benzodiazepine-induced neurological dysfunction) is a term proposed to encompass the withdrawal symptoms following long-term benzodiazepine usage and discontinuation. Pharmacist awareness of this term and confidence in its management has not been assessed. This is important to characterize, as pharmacists have a role to play in ensuring medication safety and participating in counseling and collaborative tapering. Objectives: Assess (a) Colorado pharmacist awareness of persistent benzodiazepine withdrawal symptoms following discontinuation, and (b) whether brief educational exposure would alter perceptions and confidence. Methods: This two-stage, exploratory study used data from individuals reporting long-term symptoms following benzodiazepine discontinuation to inform a survey to licensed and practicing Colorado pharmacists. Pharmacists were assessed on their knowledge of the term BIND, impression of various long-term withdrawal symptoms, tapering strategies, and responses before and after a brief educational intervention. Descriptive statistics were used for survey items, Fisher exact testing for associations between categorical variables, and the Wilcoxon Signed Ranks Test for paired pre/post Likert-Type responses. Results: 100 pharmacists initiated the survey, and 62 met the inclusion criteria. 52 of the 62 respondents that qualified completed the survey in its entirety and were included in the primary analysis. Reported item-level denominators ranged from 55 to 62. Respondents had differing knowledge of BIND and reported limited confidence in identifying and managing symptoms of withdrawal. Though education resulted in a change in pharmacist perceptions, this was not statistically significant. Pharmacists who had prior knowledge of BIND and benzodiazepine withdrawal were significantly more likely to recognize associated symptoms in their patients (reported Fisher exact P=0.011). Respondents agreed that pharmacists play a specialized role in imparting benzodiazepine education to patients and providers but varied in their confidence to do so (median of 3 on a 0-5 Likert-Type scale from not confident to very confident; n=55). Conclusions: Pharmacist awareness of BIND and long-term benzodiazepine withdrawal symptoms appear to be limited. Though brief education may not be enough to alter clinical perceptions, this study identifies gaps in knowledge and the need for additional support to help pharmacists manage patients and educate others. Future directions include a need for similar studies with larger samples, validated survey measures, and standardized educational interventions. Results should not be interpreted as the validation of BIND as a diagnosis or establishing causality between benzodiazepine exposure and patient-reported persistent symptoms.
